title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Tuberculous (TB) spondylitis, also known as Pott’s disease, represents a severe extrapulmonary manifestation of TB and remains a significant cause of morbidity worldwide. Although early disease may respond to conservative anti-TB therapy, delayed diagnosis frequently leads to progressive vertebral destruction, spinal instability, kyphotic deformity, abscess formation, and neurologic compromise. The thoracolumbar spine is most commonly affected, with children and individuals from high-incidence regions or immigrant populations at particular risk. This course reviews the diagnosis of TB spondylitis, which often proves challenging because symptoms are insidious, constitutional features are uncommon, and microbiologic confirmation may be negative, necessitating reliance on imaging, histology, and clinical suspicion, and its management, which requires prolonged chemotherapy and, in many cases, surgical intervention to decompress neural elements and restore spinal stability.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity outlines the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, imaging characteristics, and management strategies for TB spondylitis. Participants will also gain an understanding of diagnostic reasoning and the interpretation of radiologic findings, as well as the indications for medical versus surgical treatment. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying TB spondylitis, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition to optimize patient outcomes and prevent long-term complications.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Introduction
content: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide. In 2024, approximately 10.7 million people developed TB disease. Over a quarter of the world’s population has TB infection (previously designated as latent TB). [WHO. Global Tuberculosis Report 2025. 12 November 2025] TB spondylitis is an extrapulmonary form of the disease, known eponymously as Pott’s disease in recognition of the British physician, Dr. Percivall Pott, who first described the condition in 1779. [1] When diagnosed early, TB spondylitis can be treated conservatively in an effort to avoid complications. However, late diagnosis often requires both medical and surgical interventions to manage progressive bone destruction, spine instability, kyphosis, and spinal cord damage. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Tuberculosis Overview ," for further information.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Etiology
content: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) is an aerobic, nonspore-forming, and nonmotile bacterium that is the underlying causative organism of TB spondylitis. High lipid concentration within the cell wall confers acid-fast staining properties and likely plays a role in pathogenesis. They grow slowly in culture. On solid media, visible growth usually takes 3 to 8 weeks; on liquid media, visible growth usually takes 2 weeks.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Epidemiology
content: While TB occurs throughout the world, countries with the highest incidence include South-East Asia, Africa, and the Western Pacific. Osteoarticular TB accounts for approximately 1% to 15% of extrapulmonary TB, and TB spondylitis is responsible for approximately 50% to 70% of osteoarticular infections. [2] [3] In developed countries, between 5% to 90% of TB spondylitis cases occur in immigrant populations. [2] [4] Children account for approximately 50% of the population with TB spondylitis. [5]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Pathophysiology
content: The rich vascular supply of the vertebrae provides a route for MTB to disseminate from its primary focus in the lung. Dissemination to the spine can also occur via paraaortic lymphatic drainage or through the paravertebral venous plexus in genitourinary tract TB infection. Subchondral bone on either side of the intervertebral disk receives a rich blood supply, whereas the intervertebral disk is sparsely vascularized. MTB infection destroys the bony cortex of adjacent vertebral bodies and eventually the intervertebral disk. Thus, TB spondylitis tends to initially involve the paradiscal bone with destruction of the anterior spinal column, progressive anterior collapse, and concomitant separation and dislocation of posterior column structures. This results in varying degrees of spinal deformity, leading to gibbus and kyphotic deformities. The characteristics of the deformity depend on the extent of bone destruction and the number of involved vertebrae. If paravertebral soft tissues become infected, abscesses and inflammatory debris can form beneath paraspinal ligaments and within muscles. [2] [6] [7]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Pathophysiology
content: The thoracolumbar junction is most commonly involved, followed by lumbar and, less commonly, cervical vertebrae. Multilevel involvement usually involves adjacent spinal segments. Subligamentous spread can result in infection of multiple spine levels. Noncontiguous TB spondylitis can also occur via venous plexus seeding. [4]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Pathophysiology
content: Neurological complications may develop during the acute and late stages of infection. Nerve root and spinal cord compression can occur due to abscesses, granulation tissue, kyphosis, or retropulsed disk and bone. On rare occasions, thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery can develop due to adjacent inflammation. Similarly, contiguity of the meninges with the infectious process can cause myelitis, meningitis, or epidural or intradural abscesses. Cardiopulmonary compromise can develop due to severe kyphosis. When TB spondylitis involves the cervical spine, a retropharyngeal abscess may cause mediastinitis and airway obstruction.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Pathophysiology
content: TB spondylitis in children is particularly problematic due to the rapidity with which kyphosis develops in the immature spine (see Image . Thoracic Level Kyphosis in Adolescent With TB Spondylitis). Moreover, the destruction of the developing spine in children predisposes to growth retardation and to the progression of kyphosis after successful treatment. [5] [6] [8] Early onset radiculopathy and paraplegia can occur during active disease. Late-onset paraplegia due to severe deformity and spine instability can occur long after the infection has been eradicated in both children and adults. [4] [9]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Histopathology
content: Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy of the involved tissues. Based solely on histologic findings, a presumptive diagnosis can be established in approximately 60% of cases. [4] The presence of a combination of epithelioid granulomas, lymphocytic infiltration, and multinucleated giant cells is a clue to the diagnosis. Acid-fast smear positivity appears in less than 50% of cases.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- History and Physical
content: TB spondylitis progresses slowly. The presentation of patients after months to years of back pain and progressive spine deformity is not uncommon. A consistent complaint of chronic local back pain and tenderness is common and often the only symptom of TB spondylitis. However, chronic back pain is a frequently encountered complaint with a vast variety of causes. Thus, when considering TB as an etiology, obtaining a history that explores a patient’s country of origin, travel history, and potential exposures is imperative. Infants have a limited ability to convey the nature and location of their pain, making the diagnosis of TB spondylitis particularly challenging in this age group.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- History and Physical
content: Spine deformity, a late manifestation of TB spondylitis, can appear as a sharp, angular hump of the spine (ie, gibbus deformity) resulting from the collapse and wedging of vertebral bodies. Progression of vertebral collapse leads to a forward curvature of the spine (ie, kyphosis) that can range from mild to severe (see Image. Thoracic Level Kyphosis in Adolescent With TB Spondylitis). In the latter case, severe kyphosis can present with a markedly angulated and deformed spine. [4]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- History and Physical
content: Constitutional symptoms of fever, malaise, anorexia, and weight loss are uncommon features, occurring in approximately 20% to 30% of cases. The physical exam usually elicits local tenderness and may reveal stiffness and paraspinous muscle spasms. At the time of presentation, paraplegia is present in approximately 20% to 75% of patients. [4]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- History and Physical
content: Infection of the cervical spine resulting in compression of the cord or root can be associated with pain, weakness, and numbness of the extremities. If allowed to progress, paraplegia and tetraplegia can develop. Similarly, involvement of the thoracic and lumbar spine can progress to paraplegia. With involvement of the lumbo-sacral spine, compression of the cauda equina causes pain, saddle numbness, and lower extremity weakness. Bladder and bowel dysfunction can develop. Retropharyngeal abscess can cause hoarseness, dysphagia, respiratory distress, and mediastinitis. A lumbar paraspinous abscess can present as swelling of the groin, thigh, and gluteal regions.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Evaluation
content: A definitive diagnosis of TB spondylitis is established when tissue obtained by biopsy or surgery either grows the organism or tests positive by molecular probes. However, AFB stains, cultures, and molecular tests are often negative, and the diagnosis of TB spondylitis is based on a combination of radiographic findings, histology, and a high clinical suspicion. [10] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Tuberculosis Overview ," for further information on TB diagnostic criteria.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging Studies
content: Radiographic imaging is an important modality in the evaluation of suspected TB spondylitis. While radiographic features overlap with those of pyogenic infections and neoplasia, some characteristics are commonly associated with TB spondylitis. [10] [11] [12] [13] Plain x-rays are often the first modality obtained, and in resource-limited areas, they may be the only available radiographs. In the early stages of disease, x-rays may have normal findings. Reduced vertebral end-plate density, loss of vertebral height, disk space narrowing, and bone destruction are commonly identified and represent late manifestations of disease. Additionally, if present, an abscess may appear as a prevertebral fusiform soft-tissue density. [4] Approximately 60% to 70% of patients with TB spondylitis will have active pulmonary TB; thus, obtaining a chest x-ray should be a routine part of the evaluation. [6]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging Studies
content: Computed tomography (CT) can identify abnormalities earlier than plain x-rays. Abscesses, epidural lesions, and spinal cord compression are clearly visualized on CT. Calcifications within a paraspinous abscess are suggestive of TB. [4] [13] CT-guided biopsies of bone, disk, and inflammatory tissues are invaluable for evaluation and should be submitted for cytology, histology, AFB stains, culture, and nucleic acid amplification tests.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging Studies
content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most sensitive radiographic modality, capable of identifying marrow edema and disk degeneration in early stages of disease. While imaging findings are not diagnostic, a large meta-analysis identified MRI features characteristic of TB spondylitis, including: Involvement of 2 or more vertebral bodies Contiguous and noncontiguous (skip) lesions can occur Epidural extension Paravertebral collection Subligamentous spread Subligamentous abscess can extend to involve the anterior aspect of multiple vertebral bodies, with initial preservation of disks Thin-walled paraspinous muscle abscess Vertebral body collapse Kyphosis [12]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging Studies
content: Positron emission tomography (PET) can help identify the optimal site for biopsy. Furthermore, according to case reports, PET scans have been applied to help determine the adequacy and duration of anti-tuberculosis therapy. [14] Atypical imaging features can occur and delay diagnosis. Thus, emphasis should be placed on obtaining tissue as early as possible. [11] CT and MRI scans can reveal the characteristic features of TB spondylitis, including involvement of multiple contiguous and noncontiguous vertebral bodies, subligamentous abscess, and psoas abscess (see Image. CT and MRI Scans of TB Spondylitis).

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Treatment / Management
content: All patients with TB spondylitis require anti-TB chemotherapy consisting of an initial 2 months of a 4-drug intensive phase, followed by an additional 4 to 16 months of a 2-drug continuation phase regimen. The standard intensive phase consists of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. The continuation phase consists of isoniazid and rifampin. Modification of treatment regimens may be necessary based on anti-TB drug resistance and tolerability. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Tuberculosis Overview ," for further information regarding modifications to anti-TB therapy.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Treatment / Management
content: Specific recommendations for the duration of anti-TB chemotherapy vary significantly due to the wide clinical spectrum and lack of large, randomized anti-TB drug trials of TB spondylitis. [4] Consensus is lacking on which specific objective criteria should be used to determine an endpoint for chemotherapy. Knowing when to discontinue anti-TB antibiotics is particularly complicated when surgical decompression and spine instrumentation have been performed. [15] Clinical cure rate criteria, including changes in inflammatory markers, postoperative correction of kyphosis angle, bone graft fusion rate, and improvements of motor and sensory function scores, were evaluated in a large meta-analysis. [16] The study found that a 6-month regimen of anti-TB chemotherapy was comparable to regimens lasting 9 to 18 months. Whether these findings can be applied to all cases of TB spondylitis remains uncertain; in general, the current approach to treatment appears to be based on individualized criteria and the experiences of the interprofessional health care team.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical treatment of TB spondylitis is often required. In general, surgery is performed to alleviate intractable back pain and nerve compression, correct kyphosis, stabilize the spine, drain large abscesses, and, when a failure to respond to chemotherapy is present. [5] [17] Similar to the process involved in deciding on the duration of chemotherapy, as discussed above, the decision to perform surgery and the selection of the surgical procedure are not standardized. [4] Decisions regarding whether to perform anterior, posterior, a combination, or minimally invasive surgery, as well as the approach to bone grafting and internal fixation, are made based on the surgical team's experience and the patient's clinical and radiographic characteristics. Additionally, several reviews discussing the surgical indications and procedures have been published. [5] [17] [18] [19]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses that should also be considered when evaluating suspected TB spondylitis include: Chronic back pain Pyogenic spondylitis Disk abnormalities are seen more often on MRI Thick-walled abscesses are common Brucellar spondylitis Sarcoid Metastatic carcinoma Lymphoma Multiple myeloma Osteoporotic spinal fractures

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Prognosis
content: Prognosis is excellent when anti-TB therapy is initiated early, before the onset of vertebral body collapse and onset of severe neurologic deficits. [5] Several case series suggest that a good prognosis can be expected even in patients presenting with long-standing paresis and significant kyphosis. [20] [21] [22] While a complete return of function may not be achievable in all cases, partial improvement is possible when a combination of medical and surgical treatments is administered. The prognosis for neurologic recovery in children is better than in adults. Patients who have developed deficits due to spinal artery thrombosis, and those with long-standing paraplegia, are unlikely to regain neurologic function. [20]

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Resource-limited parts of the world have the highest rates of TB and TB spondylitis. Access to medical care and public health in those geographic regions is often a significant challenge. The insidious onset of symptoms, including back pain and spine deformity, frequently goes unrecognized as possible signs of TB. As a result, patients often do not seek medical attention until late in the course of the disease. Anti-TB chemotherapy is complex and requires a long duration of treatment. Compliance with therapy is often challenging and requires a commitment to patient education and government-funded public health resources.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: TB spondylitis represents the most severe manifestation of osteoarticular tuberculosis and remains a major cause of spinal deformity and neurologic disability worldwide. Insidious symptom onset and nonspecific imaging findings frequently delay diagnosis until advanced vertebral destruction, kyphosis, or spinal cord compression develops. Definitive diagnosis relies on microbiologic confirmation from biopsy or surgical specimens, although clinical suspicion and imaging often guide early management. Treatment requires prolonged multidrug anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy, with surgical intervention indicated for neurologic compromise, spinal instability, intractable pain, or severe deformity. Populations at greatest risk often face barriers to timely access to care, further complicating outcomes.

title: Tuberculous Spondylitis (Pott Disease) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management depends on coordinated interprofessional care. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners must maintain vigilance for epidemiologic risk factors and initiate appropriate diagnostic pathways. Radiologists support early recognition through careful image interpretation, while microbiologists and pathologists enable timely confirmation. Decisions regarding the need for surgical intervention require communication between the primary care clinician and the surgeon. A highly skilled surgical team is required to perform the intricately complicated surgery. Infectious disease specialists and pharmacists collaborate to guide antimicrobial selection, dosing, and monitoring. Nurses and allied health professionals ensure adherence, monitor adverse effects, and support long-term follow-up, while surgeons coordinate operative planning when indicated.
